ABW.blindSummary:
A constituent territory within a wider kingdom stands under that framework, while the territory's own criminal code, enacted in 2012, carries the anti-discrimination provisions in force here. One article defines discrimination as any form of discrimination, exclusion, restriction or preference with the purpose or effect of impairing the recognition, enjoyment or exercise of human rights and fundamental liberties in political, economic, social or cultural fields, and related articles set penalties ranging from fines to one year of imprisonment. The enumerated grounds cover heterosexual or homosexual orientation only. Gender identity and gender expression are not addressed, and no transgender-specific provision is cited in the sources.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal for both male and female forms, and the age of consent is 16, equal for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse. This is the only youth-specific legal threshold in the record; no findings on education, schools, or minors' access to services or documentation appear in the sources.

Partner recognition is established at two levels. On 8 September 2016 the territory's parliament voted 11 to 5, with four abstentions per a wire account of 9 September 2016, to extend civil-code marriage articles to registered partnerships open to both opposite-sex and same-sex couples, granting spousal pension and emergency medical decision rights. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 12 July 2024, when the supreme court of the governing state upheld an appellate decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation in the ruling that made same-sex marriage legal here. Since a ruling of that same court on 13 April 2007, the territory must recognise same-sex marriages registered in the governing state and on the neighbouring islands under the same constitutional framework. A same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2022 was rejected after tied parliamentary votes in May and June 2024, immediately before the July 2024 ruling. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship is dealing with a regime whose protections are written in terms of sexual orientation alone.

On 22 April 2015 representatives of all governments in the wider kingdom endorsed prompt equal rights for LGBT persons expressly including transgender persons on the region's island territories in the framework; the territory's own representation at that meeting acknowledged that strict conservative norms made coming out difficult for LGBT youth on the island, who were stigmatised as disordered.

Harassment has been documented. A married lesbian couple reported frequent harassment and having rocks thrown at them during their court challenge (2004-2007) that forced the territory and the other islands in the framework to recognise same-sex marriage. The territorial government was particularly vocal in opposing same-sex marriage during that court challenge, and the island's largest religious denomination contributed to mainstream societal opposition to LGBT rights. The most recent documented incident of anti-LGBT harassment in this record is from that 2004-2007 period; no later instance is documented.

Several specific gay bars and clubs operate in the capital, and various venues, hotels and restaurants cater to or advertise as 'LGBT-friendly'. Numerous LGBT associations operate, including three local equality organisations. One is quoted: 'It has always been accepting, as long as it's not in their face. People are out, but discreetly out. There has never been anything official.'
ABW.blindTangential:
The official tourism board markets the island as an established LGBT destination, positioning feeling 'safe, secure, and welcome' as the foundation of the offering and quoting a repeat visitor of nearly 20 years who reports never encountering mistreatment or discrimination based on sexual orientation. This is the destination's own marketer speaking, not independent evidence, but it documents mainstream tourism positioning.

A cultural report edited in January 2017 describes the island as tolerant and mostly open, with a smaller and quieter out-and-proud LGBT population than a neighbouring island in the same framework, and identifies the dominant religious influence as the main brake on further change. The same report notes that the government initially declared same-sex unions illegal until challenged by a lesbian couple legally married in the governing state.

Religious and cultural opposition was strong enough in 2016 that the registered-partnership bill passed only after a two-and-a-half-year campaign, and a same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2022 failed on tied parliamentary votes in May and June 2024.

Same-sex adoption is legal, per the cultural report edited in January 2017.

The registered-partnership campaign ran two and a half years, with an openly-gay legislator as sponsor, introducing the bill in August 2016, and a local equality organisation's petition at nearly 20,000 signatures.

Resident-facing organisations include three local equality organisations, alongside several gay bars and clubs in the capital.

AIA.blindSummary:
The territory is a dependent island territory whose law governs a visitor; the governing state's legislation reaches the island only where an order extends it, so no governing-state-level anti-discrimination floor applies of its own force.

Private consensual same-sex conduct was decriminalised by order of the governing state on 5 January 2001, in a decision that also covered four other island territories in the region. The order was issued unilaterally after the local legislatures refused to repeal their statutes, and religious leaders protested the decision. The territory had never carried the prohibition in exactly the same statutory form as those other territories.

Local law provides no protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The constitution's anti-discrimination clause reaches race, political opinions, colour, creed, sex and place of origin, so gender identity sits outside the protected categories and a trans visitor has no statutory non-discrimination footing in local law.

The age of consent is 18 for same-sex conduct and 16 for different-sex conduct. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship therefore carries legal exposure that a different-sex couple does not face.

The marriage law defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman as husband and wife. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal, and no civil-partnership legislation has been enacted here. A commercial destination-wedding service marketing ceremonies on the island states that same-sex marriage is not recognised under local law, so a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has access only to a symbolic, non-legal ceremony. Non-legal ceremonies of same-sex couples have taken place there.

Public LGBT life is highly constrained. A subdued and subtle climate of homophobia has pushed local LGBT people toward secrecy. The island has no pride events, gay organisations, venues, bars or clubs and no community infrastructure, which the source attributes to a population of about 15,000. The only recorded public event is a small protest on 17 May 2011 in the capital marking the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia.

Visiting same-sex couples have described the island as gay-friendly and reported that nobody was discriminatory in any way, though the same source cautions that the position of local people may differ. A 2023 first-person account by a queer family found same-sex conduct legal under the governing state's order but the scene muted rather than openly visible, an outcome that account attributes to decriminalisation imposed from outside rather than to local initiative.
AIA.blindTangential:
The 2001 decriminalisation came from the governing state rather than from the local legislature, and it covered five territories at once. The absence of partnership recognition here is a pattern across several territories in the same constitutional family rather than a measure specific to this island.

The island is small and remote, with about 15,000 residents. The 2012 country report and the 2023 travel account both tie the absence of any LGBT venue, organisation or pride event to that small scale at least as much as to enforcement or legal prohibition.

Accounts written for visitors describe a relaxed reception for visiting same-sex couples while the material on residents describes secrecy and a subdued climate of homophobia. The two bodies of evidence describe different populations, and the visitor material was produced by couples on holiday rather than by residents.
AIA.blindLocalsOnly:
Residents have no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The constitution's protected grounds are race, political opinions, colour, creed, sex and place of origin.

The age of consent for same-sex conduct is 18, against 16 for different-sex conduct, a differential that applies to residents as well as to visitors.

Marriage under the marriage law is the union of a man and a woman as husband and wife. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and civil partnerships are not available, and couples can hold only symbolic ceremonies.

Local LGBT people are described as pushed toward secrecy by a subdued and subtle climate of homophobia. There are no pride events, gay organisations, bars, clubs or venues and no community infrastructure, which the sources attribute to a population of roughly 15,000. No trans-specific organisation, support service or venue appears in the sources either. The one recorded public event is a small protest in the capital on 17 May 2011 marking the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia.

Decriminalisation was imposed by order of the governing state after the local legislature declined to repeal the prohibition, and it drew protest from religious leaders.
AIA.blindOutOfScope:
No source in the inventory sets out local rules on gender markers on identity documents, on entry or immigration screening, or on access to sex-segregated facilities. Those questions are unresolved here.

No trans-specific violence data and no hate-crime enforcement data were identified, and the inventory contains no general homicide denominator for the island, so no risk magnitude for anti-trans violence can be stated.

Sources give different years for decriminalisation: the 2023 travel account states a year earlier than the governing state's order, which is dated 5 January 2001, and the encyclopaedic coverage gives 2001. The 2001 date is the documented one.

Whether any order has extended the governing state's anti-discrimination legislation to the territory is not established in the inventory. The sources identify the mechanism but name no such order.

The favourable accounts of how visiting same-sex couples were treated describe a different population from the residents covered by the material on secrecy and lack of protection, and the sources themselves caution that local conditions may differ from the visitor experience. No source reports how a visibly trans visitor, as distinct from a same-sex couple, was received.

ASM.blindSummary:
The territory's own criminal code does not punish consensual sodomy. The first sodomy statute, enacted in 1963, covered male homosexual and heterosexual conduct and did not address lesbian conduct; the territorial legislature's 1979 revision, effective in 1980, retained prohibition only for public acts, prostitution, conduct involving minors and conduct with persons unable to consent. The age of consent is 16, regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

Same-sex marriage is not licensed. On 20 March 2003 the legislature's upper chamber rejected a bill, introduced by a legislator, that would have outlawed it, after a committee recommended the bill be killed; at the committee hearing a fa'afafine resident testified that fa'afafine do not seek marriage with men, describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech and citing Christian upbringing. In July 2015 the territory's chief legal officer was reviewing whether the governing state's top court 2015 marriage-equality ruling reached the territory and said he did not know, while the governor stated that it did not apply, citing the territory's preamble, its constitution, Christian values and its unorganised and unincorporated political status. No same-sex couple had filed an application at that point, and a 2026 law-review article by two attorneys practising in the territory records that none has applied since.

In January 2016 the upper chamber unanimously confirmed a former chief legal officer as a district court judge after he told confirming senators, including a retired judge-senator, that he had not read the 2015 ruling, that the district court does not deal with it, and that he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws change.

In July 2024 an on-island survey by a constitutional and comparative law professor tested whether the territory's ban would survive a challenge under the governing state's constitutional equality provisions. As of mid-2024 the ban is treated locally as operative and its constitutional durability as an open question. The 2026 article reaches the opposite conclusion on the law, holding that the 2015 ruling does apply despite those official statements and that the territory would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied; it sets out a litigation path through the territory's high court first, with the territory's registrar as defendant, then the governing state's interior ministry. Since 13 December 2022 the territory has been obliged to recognise, though not perform, same-sex marriages performed legally in another jurisdiction, with equal treatment for same-sex and opposite-sex couples.

The territory's marriage code does not specify the sex of the parties. It refers to the age of 'the male' and 'the female' on a form in which parties identify as 'son' and as 'daughter'.

Gender markers on local documents are changeable within limits. The territory's high court has held that birth certificates may be altered only to correct information that was erroneous at the time of recordation or to reflect a name change due to adoption, and the civil records office reads that ruling as covering applications from transgender people: it changes the name on a birth certificate when presented with a name change order, and may change the gender marker with medical documentation of the sex change.

Documented trans-specific legal matters in the territory concern employment and criminal proceedings. In June 2023 a federal civil action cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity, and in September 2023 the governing state's federal law-enforcement department secured a settlement with the territorial government resolving an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee. In February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teenager; that charge is the most recent documented instance of violence against a trans person in this record, no later instance is documented, and no outcome for the charge is stated.

Public climate combines cultural recognition with religious conservatism. Fa'afafine, defined as people born male who embody both male and female traits, are described in local scholarship as a recognised and integral part of traditional culture, and a fa'afafine community organisation, formed in 2010, campaigns for the community and runs annual events; the first Pride festival was held in August 2016, and beauty pageants among the fa'afafine community draw family support. Society is nonetheless highly religious, conservative attitudes on gender and sexuality dominate, and open displays of affection between couples, same-sex or opposite-sex, may offend. A 2009 travel column described reserved public behaviour as expected of people of all orientations in the territory.

That comparison is dated 10 July 2015 and describes the position at that time.

The 2003 bill's defeat means the territory deliberately declined to enact a formal same-sex marriage ban before the 2015 ruling, and the committee record preserves contemporaneous fa'afafine testimony opposing such a ban on religious grounds rather than on grounds of marriage rights.

A 2009 travel column contrasted the territory with a neighbouring Pacific jurisdiction, describing homosexuality as widely accepted in the island culture while noting that reserved public behaviour is expected, and reported that hotels near the main town skew toward business travel. The column is a publication's own framing and is now more than fifteen years old.

The 2026 law-review article is the most recent dated authority on whether the 2015 ruling is operative here, and it separates the law as written from the practical reality of an untested statute book. No court in the territory has decided the question.
ASM.blindLocalsOnly:
A fa'afafine community organisation was formed in 2010 by merging two earlier community groups and re-anchored its identity to cultural pride. It campaigns for the community and runs annual events; the first Pride festival took place in August 2016 with pageant, song, dance and poetry competitions, and beauty pageants among the fa'afafine community draw family support in numbers.

Residents have obtained relief in the employment sphere: a June 2023 federal civil action alleged a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's suit against the territorial government, and in September 2023 the governing state's federal law-enforcement department settled an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee with the territorial government.

Residents seeking to amend a birth certificate deal with the civil records office, which changes the name when presented with a name change order and may change the gender marker on medical documentation of the sex change, reading the high court's ruling to cover transgender applications even though the ruling itself addresses only erroneous information and adoption-related name changes.

The territory's own legislative and academic record is active on the marriage question: the legislature rejected a ban in 2003, a constitutional law professor surveyed the community in July 2024, and local attorneys published the 2026 analysis. Fa'afafine are described in local scholarship as an integral part of traditional culture, and a long-standing practice of raising some boys to fill a domestic role is documented, alongside a highly religious society in which conservative attitudes on gender and sexuality dominate.

The 2026 law-review article says it does and that a certificate would have to be issued; the territory's governor and judiciary have acted on the premise that it does not. No court has ruled, and no same-sex couple is documented as having applied for a licence at any point.

No outcome is stated for the February 2023 sexual-abuse charge involving a 16-year-old transgender teenager, and no later instance of violence against a trans person is documented in this inventory. Whether further incidents occurred and were not recorded is not sourced either way.

No source in this inventory reports a refusal by the civil records office to change a gender marker, or any appeal from such a refusal, so the practical limits of the medical-documentation requirement are not sourced.

The governing state's passport policy and its 2025 executive orders on sex definition, healthcare funding and sports are not restated here; they are carried at the national level of the governing state's record. This summary covers only the territory's own laws, institutions and documented events.

No figure is available for the prevalence of discrimination complaints, police reporting, or public attitudes toward trans people in the territory; the 2024 survey tested constitutional durability, not incidence.

BES.blindSummary:
Three special-municipality islands stand under the governing state's national framework: the governing state's civil-status and anti-discrimination law applies here in the same form, with no separate island legislation on marriage or discrimination operating alongside it. The governing state's framework applies directly.

No source in the inventory describes a provision that addresses trans visitors directly. The protection that exists on these islands is carried by marriage registration and general anti-discrimination law, not by text naming gender identity, gender markers or facilities.

A small island's registry recorded the island group's first same-sex union on 4 December 2012: two visiting residents, one from a sibling island in the same framework and one from a South American country, wed on the island. Same-sex unions have therefore been registrable in these islands since 2012, and the island registry has performed one for visitors. This 2012 registration is the only dated union event in the sources; no later instance is documented.

For a trans visitor whose relationship would be read locally as same-sex, that registration evidences a working route rather than a paper right. Civil ceremonies run through the island registry, with the courthouse room in the administrative building recorded as the simplest venue for an efficient ceremony and one registrar documented as flexible about couples' wishes. Full destination-wedding suppliers, including caterers, florists and accommodation, operate on the island.

This is a publication's editorial framing, not a measurement of risk, enforcement or trans-specific conditions, and it makes no finding about gender identity, markers or facilities.

The inventory contains no comparative figure for these islands against other jurisdictions in the region on trans-specific violence, screening practice or legal recognition, so no ranking of the islands' relative safety can be drawn from it.
BES.blindLocalsOnly:

The island registry performs civil ceremonies as a routine public function, documented through its official tourism service, and it registered a union for two visiting residents on 4 December 2012. Residents seeking recognition of a relationship classed locally as same-sex use the same registry route.
BES.blindOutOfScope:

The 4 December 2012 union is the only dated registration event in the sources; no later instance is documented, and the absence of later records is not evidence either way about current practice.

BLM.blindSummary:
The island is an overseas collectivity of the governing state, and the governing state's national framework applies here as on its mainland: its criminal law, identity documents, anti-discrimination statute and marriage regime govern the island.

Medical capacity is the sharpest practical constraint. The island covers about 8 square miles and holds roughly 10,000 residents, and the single recorded red flag in an aggregate travel-safety rating is limited healthcare access. Prescriptions and ongoing gender-affirming treatment cannot be assumed to be available locally, and a visitor who depends on either should carry supplies and confirm provision before arrival.

Anyone detained on the island falls under the governing state's prison administration, whose placement policy recognises only biological sex; trans detainees, overwhelmingly women, are held under birth sex. The governing state's detention watchdog, in an opinion of 25 May 2021 drawing on about 40 referrals received since 2010, found that serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, with recommendations that also cover intersex and non-binary persons.

Socially the island is discreet rather than permissive. It has no LGBTQ venues, no Pride events and no visible scene; same-sex couples attract no attention, crime is low, and the sources record no hostility toward gay or trans visitors. The luxury-yacht economy has long welcomed gay couples, and hospitality staff are described as trained for a diverse clientele.

Politically, the island's joint deputy with a neighbouring island collectivity was among a group of overseas deputies who voted against the governing state's 2013 law opening marriage to same-sex couples.
BLM.blindTangential:
Among the governing state's island territories in the region, the island's standing as an international celebrity destination is credited with a more open and relaxed social climate for LGBTQ people than the larger neighbouring overseas territories.

The island's small size and its dependence on a luxury-tourism economy shape both the absence of an organised scene and the discretion expected of visitors, in contrast to the larger territories nearby.
BLM.blindLocalsOnly:
Residents who need ongoing gender-affirming care face the same capacity limit that constrains visitors: the island's small size and population support only limited medical services, and specialist provision is not assured locally.

The collectivity's representation in the national legislature voted against the 2013 marriage law, and the island has no LGBTQ venue, Pride event or visible organising of its own.
BLM.blindOutOfScope:
No government LGBT+ travel advice specific to the island exists, and a foreign government's travel service records no warnings for the collectivity. No trans-specific visitor tips have been submitted to the aggregate index.

The aggregate travel-safety rating is a composite score rather than a legal finding, and its components are not itemised in the source; its numerical value is not reproduced here.

Accounts of the island's LGBTQ infrastructure conflict: one source lists gay bars, discos, saunas and beaches among the governing state's island territories in the region including this one, while island-level guides report no LGBTQ venue or scene. The discrepancy is unresolved.
blindSourceSummaries: Reporting on the governing state's prison system: its detention administration places trans detainees, overwhelmingly women held under birth-sex placement; administration policy recognises only biological sex (a 2011 case placed a trans woman in a men's prison). The island's detainees fall under this system.

The governing state's detention watchdog's opinion of 25 May 2021 on transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty draws on about 40 referrals since 2010; it finds serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, with recommendations applicable also to intersex and non-binary persons.

A rights compilation: the governing state's framework applies here - legal gender-marker change without surgery or sterilisation, hormone therapy and surgery available since 1975, anti-discrimination coverage; non-binary recognition limited.

A travel-safety profile: full equality under the governing state's law applies across about 8 square miles and about 10,000 residents; the luxury-yacht economy has long welcomed gay couples, with no visible scene; discretion is the norm and same-sex couples attract no attention; the single recorded red flag is limited healthcare access.

A travel guide: low crime, an open and accepting culture, no Pride-specific events, and staff trained for diverse guests; visitors are high-end and discreet; there are no LGBTQ venues or scene, and no hostility is noted.

A legal note: the governing state banned discrimination on the basis of 'sexual identity' in July 2012 and replaced that term with 'gender identity' by the law of 18 November 2016 amending the penal code; the labour code prohibits exclusion from recruitment, internships or training and sanction, dismissal or discriminatory measures on that account.

BMU.blindSummary:
The island is a dependent island territory of the governing state in which local legislation governs; the governing state's statutes do not extend automatically. The territory has no legal recognition of transgender people. The human-rights act has prohibited discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation since 2013, when the legislature's upper chamber passed the amendment act, which also banned age discrimination; gender identity is not a protected ground, so trans people have no statutory protection against discrimination. Proposals to extend that protection were failed or dropped in 2004-2006 and again in 2009.

The sources identify no territory-specific provisions on identity documents or gender markers, border or airport screening, restroom and facility access, custody, healthcare, penalties or protection machinery for transgender people. The absence of gender identity as a protected ground is the only trans-specific legal finding the record carries.

The record describes expression of gender identity as often difficult and documents one instance of official interference: in 2006 the government attempted to bar a drag performer from participating in a parade, stating that he contradicted local mores and sensitivities. CUW.blindSummary:
The island is an autonomous constituent country within a wider kingdom, with full autonomy except in defence, foreign affairs and matters reserved to the kingdom's supreme court.

Both male and female same-sex sexual activity is legal, with an equal age of consent of 16 for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse. A trans visitor in a relationship read locally as same-sex faces no conduct offence on that basis.

Same-sex marriage has been legal on the island since 12 July 2024, when the kingdom's supreme court upheld an appellate decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation. Before that ruling, the island recognised as valid same-sex marriages registered in the governing state and on the nearby special-municipality islands, but offered no in-island marriage, civil union or other form of recognition.

Recognition arrived by court order rather than by statute. A limited-rights proposal was put to the island's legislature in 2017, and a marriage bill submitted on 4 June 2019 was withdrawn in September 2020 for lack of support. In April 2015 representatives of all governments in the wider kingdom agreed that LGBT people on the region's island territories in the framework should receive equal rights quickly, and an August 2015 judgment of the international human-rights court, applicable here, required legal recognition.

The criminal code enacted in 2011 prohibits unfair discrimination and incitement to hatred and violence on grounds that include heterosexual or homosexual orientation. One article defines discrimination as any distinction affecting the recognition, enjoyment or exercise of human rights in political, economic, social, cultural or other social life, and related articles set penalties ranging from fines to one year of imprisonment. The protected grounds named in the source material do not include gender identity, and no island-specific authority on gender-identity coverage was identified.

Official rhetoric has not consistently governed practice. In April 2015 a government commissioner publicly backed equal rights for everyone in the local press, while a party colleague opposed the rights push fiercely and used a last-minute, exceptionally strict permit requirement to force the island's 2013 Gay Pride to relocate to a hotel premises. Public LGBT assembly on the island can be obstructed through administrative permitting at short notice.

The island opened an LGBT community centre in 2010, and alongside its sibling territories has acted as a driver of equal-rights moves across the kingdom. A local pride organiser cites a travel-association award naming the island welcoming to gay visitors, and a rights wishes-package was delivered to ministers in the governing state's capital.

No island-specific sourcing was found on gender markers in locally issued identity documents, entry or border screening triggered by gender presentation, access to gender-affirming care, or the designation of facilities. Those areas are unassessed rather than cleared.

CYM.blindSummary:
The territory's constitutional discrimination grounds were drafted in 2009 without sexual-orientation protection. Public visibility in the tourist-facing environment is high. Around 600 people, among them the premier, the governor, ministers and members of the legislature, joined a local LGBT foundation's first Pride parade on 7 August 2021, with broad official participation.

ESH.blindSummary:
The disputed territory has no single legal order running through it. An administering state controls most of the ground and its security services, courts and detention facilities operate there; a movement claiming sovereignty governs through exile institutions and refugee camps across the border in a neighbouring country. Which framework a visitor stands under depends on which part of the territory they are in.

The administering state's jurisdiction reaches into the territory in practice. On 9 December 2005 an international human-rights organisation reported the trial of seven human-rights defenders from the administered part on charges of fomenting illegal protests, called the charges dubious and demanded a fair trial. The case shows the administering state's courts and detention operating on political cases from the territory, not only on paper.

Same-sex intimacy is criminalised under both frameworks. The administering state's law carries six months to three years of imprisonment. For the movement's self-proclaimed state, international monitors record same-sex sexual activity as illegal for both men and women, punishable by up to three years, and a July 2017 global legality roundup listed it among jurisdictions where homosexuality is illegal for men and women and had been for decades. A trans visitor in a relationship that local law would read as same-sex under birth-sex status therefore stands inside a criminal prohibition in either part of the territory.

The movement's own position is contested. In 2010 its diplomatic representative in a country in the region said its constitution 'does not refer to homosexuality or any other sexual practice... it does not punish it'. A refugee-aid organisation reads the same silence as leaving LGBTQ people with no legal protection against discrimination or violence. Constitutional silence is not decriminalisation, and no statute in the inventory decriminalises anything.

The only documented account of the movement's authorities applying such charges comes from a 2009 refugee-policy report: officials running the refugee camps said they were holding some prisoners on 'homosexuality' charges while alleging facts that would more fittingly describe rape. The charge sits in the hands of camp administration rather than a court.

Social exposure is high. Most residents are Muslim, and relationships between people of the same sex are widely read as a foreign phenomenon.

No source in the inventory records a trans-specific statute, a protection mechanism, or a documented case of a trans visitor being processed under either framework.

FRO.blindSummary:

In 2006 an openly gay singer, songwriter and radio host was severely beaten by five men in the capital and hospitalised shortly after coming out; he and his family then received threatening telephone calls, and police refused to handle the case because no local law banned discrimination against sexual minorities at the time. He was later moved to a psychiatric hospital with severe depression exacerbated by the beating, never recovered, and died by suicide in 2012. The most recent documented assault in this record is that 2006 attack; no later instance is documented.

The island nonetheless retains specific male homosexual offences in its criminal law, including a ban on homosexual sexual acts not conducted in private, which can expose men to prosecution for private-life conduct that is lawful elsewhere.

Transgender people have been able to legally change their gender since 2007, including obtaining a new birth certificate. Local law only allows a new birth certificate to be issued and does not amend or remove records from existing birth certificates, so prior gender markers remain on the original record.

No civil-partnership legislation has been enacted on the island, though civil partnerships from the governing state were recognised for succession purposes from 2 April 2012. The island's parliament approved same-sex marriage on 10 December 2015 by a vote of 37 to 7, rejecting both a civil-partnership-only option and a single 'Union Civile' alternative; implementing legislation was to be separate and was not expected before 2017.

A 2004 law enabled the island's parliament to pass ordinances banning discrimination, and the 2005 sex discrimination (employment) ordinance banned discrimination based on gender identity. As of 2020 no equivalent ordinance had specifically outlawed discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. Anti-discrimination protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity existed in child welfare proceedings on the main island and its smaller inhabited islands since 2008 and on one smaller island since 2016. In September 2022 the parliament passed a comprehensive anti-discrimination bill unanimously (33-0) explicitly including sexual orientation, rejecting all amendments proposing exemptions for small businesses of five employees or fewer and for religious affiliations; it takes effect from 1 October 2023.

The island's only prison, opened in 1989, holds male, female and vulnerable prisoners of juvenile and adult ages; it has 11 wings, capacity 139, is operated by the island's government, and held about 99 prisoners in November 2024. No rule on housing prisoners by birth sex versus gender identity, no separate unit for trans prisoners, and no solitary or segregation practice for them is recorded.

The parliament repealed the 50-year-old adoption law's ban on unmarried couples adopting on 24 June 2015, agreeing that same-sex couples may adopt, with civil partnerships recognised and equal parental responsibility for both partners; a neighbouring island dependency approved the same change two days earlier. The parliament's formal policy paper of 24 June 2015 records the review of adoption law that led to adoption rights for same-sex couples.

The island adopted the governing state's relaxed blood-donor rules on 23 September 2011, making gay and bisexual men eligible after a 12-month deferral, targeted to around 7 November 2011 to match the governing state's change, ending the local 1980s HIV-era ban; other donation restrictions were unchanged.

GIB.blindSummary:
The territory is self-governing with its own parliament and its own supreme court, which make and interpret its civil and criminal law. Measures enacted by the governing state do not apply of their own force: that state's equality act and the single-sex-services code issued in 2025 bind the territory only if extended by an order of the governing state, and no such extension appears in the sourced material.

The principal legal gap facing a trans visitor is gender recognition. No process exists here for changing a legal gender marker, and the sourced material records that transgender persons are not permitted to change legal gender. A trans visitor therefore travels on a document whose marker cannot be altered by any local route, and can expect to be read at the border and in public under that marker.

Statutory discrimination protection covering gender reassignment has been in place since the 2006 equal opportunities act took effect on 1 March 2007. The act prohibits discrimination in employment and in the provision of goods and services on the ground of gender reassignment, defined as a process for the purpose of reassigning a person's sex by changing physiological or other attributes of sex. Sexual orientation is a protected ground under the same act.

Hate-crime coverage extends to trans people. Parliament amended the 2011 crimes act in September 2013 to criminalise hatred and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, with approval on 19 September, formal assent on 25 September and effect from 10 October 2013. In July 2026 parliament passed a bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to include protections for transgender identity.

In July 2021 the justice ministry said it would urgently consider legislation to tackle what the head of government called 'disgusting lurking homophobia' on social media during Pride month, following an incident of anti-gay abuse. The proposal at that stage concerned sexual orientation; the trans-inclusive amendment came in July 2026.

In July 2026 parliament also passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practise conversion therapy. The sourced excerpt states the offence generally without specifying whether its scope covers sexual orientation, transgender identity, or both.

Partner recognition is established locally. Civil partnerships have been available since March 2014, and same-sex marriage since 15 December 2016, after the civil marriage amendment act passed unanimously on 26 October 2016, received assent on 1 November and took effect on 15 December, with the first marriage the following day. A deputy registrar may opt out, requiring assignment of an alternative registrar. Because no gender-recognition route exists, a trans visitor's legal sex for marriage purposes remains that recorded at birth; a relationship locally read as same-sex can be registered.

Adoption is open to same-sex couples. The supreme court ruled on 10 April 2013 that a section of the 1951 adoption act violated the territory's constitution, and the 2023 adoption act took full effect on 18 April 2024, expressly allowing same-sex couples to adopt without discrimination.

The age of consent is 16 for all sexual activity regardless of sexuality or gender. The supreme court ruled on 8 April 2011 that the previous age of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional, and the gender-neutral 2011 crimes act, approved in August 2011, set the equal age of 16 with effect from 23 November 2012.

A private member's bill to equalise the age of consent was defeated in parliament on 18 May 2009, two years before the supreme court ruled the higher age unconstitutional.

The 2006 constitution does not mention sexual orientation; proposals in 2002 omitted it.

The 2016 marriage reform followed a December 2015 consultation that left the public polarized. A government minister presided over an inter-ministerial committee weighing all viewpoints, and the main parties indicated support for the change.

GRL.blindSummary:
The territory is self-governing within the governing state's realm. Its parliament and courts handle domestic affairs, while the governing state's legislation on marriage and on official identity documents has been adopted and applies here. A visitor's legal position on those questions follows that framework as received locally.

Same-sex relations carry no criminal penalty. Since 2010 article 100 of the criminal code has prohibited speech that may deprive, threaten or demean people on the basis of sexual orientation among other protected categories, and the code provides penalty enhancement for hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation. No prosecution under either provision is recorded in the available sources.

Same-sex marriage took effect on 1 April 2016, adopting the governing state's legislation that passed unanimously on two occasions after the first bill lapsed in elections in that state. It replaced the registered partnership that had run from 1 July 1996, whose application was repealed the day the marriage law commenced. The bishop of the established church supported the change. Marriage is available to a trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status.

Legal change of sex designation on official documents rests on self-determination. The law, passed in 2016 and brought into force by decree, requires no sex reassignment surgery, hormone therapy, sterilization or medical diagnosis. Applicants must be over 18 and state that they want their documentation changed, then observe a six-month reflection period to confirm the request.

Local passports are issued with an X sex descriptor in addition to male and female.

The law on equal treatment and anti-discrimination was passed by the parliament in May 2024 and took effect on 1 July 2024. It prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and gender characteristics, among other characteristics. It creates an equal treatment board to handle discrimination complaints and an equality council to promote non-discrimination.

Public expression is visible. The first pride parade was held in the main town on 15 May 2010 and drew about 1,000 people, and a modest march has continued since. Accounts from 2015 describe gay life as low-key, integrated and non-violent, with no reported anti-LGBT violence.

The small, scattered population supports almost no dedicated gay scene. Some nightclubs and bars in the main town draw a mixed gay and straight crowd.

GUF.blindSummary:

Detention carries the most serious documented risk. Specialist gender-affirming care is not provided locally on the same basis as on the governing state's mainland. Patients travel to the mainland for surgery and specialist assessment, and the journey adds cost and delay to every medical step, including any undertaken during a stay in the department.

Transphobia and cultural taboos discourage visibility in the department, and abuse is less likely to be reported, including to the police. Under-reporting is a feature of the local situation rather than evidence that abuse is rare.

GUM.blindSummary:
The island's own law governs legal gender recognition, and it requires surgery. To amend a birth certificate, a transgender person must give the civil records office a sworn statement from a physician confirming sex reassignment surgery, after which the office amends the certificate. The licensing authority issues an amended driver's licence on receipt of a sworn physician statement that the applicant's sex has been surgically changed.

A 2018 attempt to remove the surgery requirement failed. A legislator introduced a bill in May 2018 to permit legal gender change on judicial permission with a letter confirming gender identity supported by documentation from a certified psychologist, social worker, therapist or other licensed professional, with no surgery required. The legislature postponed a vote on 13 December 2018 pending medical and law enforcement process issues, and the bill failed on 17 December 2018 by a 6 to 7 vote. Surgery remains the condition for both documents.

Marriage recognition for a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship rests on the 2015 ruling. The chief judge struck down the island's prohibition on same-sex marriage in June 2015 after an April 2015 lawsuit by a couple who had been denied a marriage licence. The ruling took effect at 8am on Tuesday 9 June 2015.

Private consensual adult non-commercial sexual conduct has been lawful since the 1978 reform of the criminal code; the penal code in force before that, ordained in 1933, had criminalised sodomy, fellatio and cunnilingus with between one and ten years' imprisonment.

The island hosts a large permanent military presence of the governing state, so that state's federal policy on transgender service members bears directly on personnel stationed on the island.

A visible LGBTQ social scene has existed since the 1990s, with a handful of nightclubs and social functions and an annual Pride held since 2017 attracting a few hundred people. The island is a member of an international gay and lesbian travel association and has begun marketing itself as a tourist destination for LGBTQ people.

IMN.blindSummary:
The island is a self-legislating dependency. Its parliament enacts its own statutes on gender recognition, equality and criminal law, and the governing state's legislation reaches the island only when extended by an order of that state rather than automatically.

The 2009 gender recognition act allows transgender people to change their legal gender and to have the new gender recognised. The 2017 equality act, granted assent on 18 July 2017 and largely in force from 1 January 2019, lists gender reassignment as a protected characteristic and as a ground on which discrimination is prohibited.

A ban on conversion therapy covering sexual orientation and gender identity was passed in 2020 as an amendment to the sexual offences bill in the legislature's upper chamber and took effect in 2024. The sourced account presents the prohibition as an early move within the governing state's family of jurisdictions.

In July 2022 community consultation progressed on a hate crime bill that would explicitly include gender reassignment alongside sexual orientation and marital or civil partnership status. The bill's status after that consultation is not sourced.

Sexual offences law applies gender-neutrally. Private consensual male homosexual acts were decriminalised in September 1992 with an age of consent of twenty-one, lowered to eighteen by the 2001 criminal justice act, then lowered to sixteen and made gender-neutral for all sexual conduct regardless of gender and sexual orientation by the 2006 sexual offences amendment. Until 2021, a section of the 1992 sexual offences act retained offences of buggery and gross indecency between men if under sixteen or committed elsewhere than in private; in 2021 the more-than-two-persons specification was deleted and language on indecent exposure and sexual activity in a public place was made gender-neutral under a 2021 act, which received assent in July 2021 and took effect on 1 July 2022 by proclamation.

On partner recognition, same-sex couples have held civil partnerships since 6 April 2011 under the 2011 civil partnership act, and marriage has been available since 22 July 2016 following assent on 19 July 2016. Existing civil partnerships could be converted without a second ceremony, and the first conversion was completed within days of entry into force. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be locally classed as same-sex enters a jurisdiction that recognises the union.

Family law has not kept pace with that recognition. Under the 2011 civil partnership act, same-sex couples have had equal access to full joint or stepchild adoption since 6 April 2011 and lesbian couples have access to artificial insemination, but as of an August 2023 consultation same-sex couples are not recognised as parents on birth certificates in cases of IVF and surrogacy, and no law on the island acknowledges surrogacy.
IMN.blindTangential:
The primary legislative record of the island's marriage-equality debate is the parliament's official report of 26 April 2016, which covers the upper chamber's third reading of the 2016 marriage bill and consideration of the 2016 equality bill.

The reform sequence is documented: the head of government publicly backed same-sex marriage on 9 June 2015 and said he would formulate a bill to repeal the island's marriage prohibition, the political commitment that preceded the marriage act in force from 22 July 2016.

The 2024 conversion-therapy prohibition is presented in the sources as an early move among the governing state's family of jurisdictions and within the island's region on that measure, a comparison the sources state explicitly rather than a ranking derived from incident counts.
IMN.blindLocalsOnly:
Employment protection on sexual orientation predates the 2017 equality act: the legislature's lower chamber adopted an employment bill amendment on 30 November 2005 protecting gay and lesbian employees from dismissal on sexual-orientation grounds, tabled by a legislator, and the 2006 employment act made dismissal on those grounds unlawful with effect from 1 September 2006.

The 2017 equality act lists sexual orientation as a protected characteristic and defines it to include attraction to the same, opposite or either sex and lack of attraction to either sex.

A 2021 act pardoned historical gay sex offences committed before 1992, explicitly modelled on the governing state's 2017 pardons law. The head of government issued an unqualified apology to gay men convicted under previous laws, and in August 2022, on the thirtieth anniversary of decriminalisation, the police commissioner formally apologised for enforcement of anti-gay laws up to 1992.
IMN.blindOutOfScope:

MYT.blindSummary:

Trans detainees in the island's establishments are held according to the gender shown on their identity document under the governing state's criminal procedure code, which in practice places trans women in all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them; placement follows the document marker rather than anatomy.

The governing state's detention watchdog reported on 25 May 2021 a persistence of serious violations of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across all of that state's places of deprivation of liberty, based on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons and on-site inspections in which eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed at four mainland establishments. Legal gender change without surgery, forced sterilisation, psychiatric certificates or proof of medical intervention was approved by the senate on 6 November 2015 and the national assembly on 24 May 2016, modified on 12 July 2016 to drop self-certification, re-approved on 12 October, ruled constitutional on 17 November, signed 18 November 2016 and effective 1 January 2017; a court appearance is still required to change the gender marker, while a first-name change can be done at the registry office. National law bans discrimination on the basis of gender identity: the penal code was amended on 18 November 2016 to replace 'sexual identity' with 'gender identity', and the labour code prohibits exclusion from recruitment, internships or training and sanction, dismissal or discriminatory measures on that account. Since 2017 transphobia has been an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by prison.

Formal entitlement and lived experience diverge. A teacher at the island's university centre and his partner from a neighbouring island country married at a town hall on the island in 2023, after what reporting described as a long and complicated path, on a predominantly Muslim island where the written law is not the whole of what a couple faces. Same-sex marriage has been legal here since the island voted to remain part of the governing state in 1975.

Legal representation is thinly available locally. Same-sex unions are not recognised on the island even though they are recognised in the governing state, and section 6 of the 2022 family relationships act expressly prohibits same-sex marriage. Couples and households headed by such couples are not eligible for the legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples. A trans visitor whose relationship would be classified locally as same-sex has no route to recognition or to the protections attached to marriage.

The 2010 constitution order has prohibited discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation since 2010. The guarantee is constitutional rather than an offence provision, and it names sexual orientation and not gender identity, so a trans visitor has no express constitutional protection on gender-identity grounds.

The 2015 marriage and civil-partnerships ordinance made same-sex marriage legal on 14 May 2015 and defines marriage as the union of two people regardless of sex, sexual orientation or gender identity. That definition is the only express reference to gender identity in the territory's legislation recorded in these sources. The ordinance was approved unanimously by the island council on 1 April 2015, signed by the governor on 5 May 2015 and published on 13 May 2015.

The same ordinance recognises civil partnerships performed outside the islands, so a partnership or marriage entered abroad is recorded as recognised locally.

No incident of violence targeting a trans person is documented for the islands in these sources, and no dated case of any kind appears in the record.

The territory's discrimination guarantee and its marriage law are the two instruments that carry weight for a trans visitor, and they differ in scope: the constitution covers sexual orientation only, while the 2015 marriage definition expressly covers gender identity. The sources rank no jurisdictions and provide no comparative or per-capita figures for the islands, so no comparison of risk levels between territories can be drawn from this record.

PRI.blindSummary:
The territory stands under the governing state's federal framework for entry, documents, federally funded care and federal custody; the findings below are the territory's own law, its own enforcement and its own institutions.

A 2025 minors' wellbeing law (Law 63 of 2025), enacted in July 2025, bars gender-affirming care for anyone under 21, withdraws public funding for that care, and penalises violations with a fixed 15-year prison term, a $50,000 fine per violation for legal persons, and permanent loss of medical licences for professionals. Its article 4, the operative prohibition, is directed at medical institutions and health professionals: none may perform surgical interventions or medication treatments that alter sex biology under the pretext of gender transition or as part of gender-dysphoria treatment.

Article 3 defines the banned chemical and surgical practice more broadly than the operative clause. It expressly names the use of puberty blockers and sex hormones, including androgen blockers, oestrogen, progesterone or testosterone, when used to treat gender dysphoria, and it sets the protected class at anyone under 21. Article 6 penalises any person who violates the law's provisions.

The gap between a definition framed around patient use and an operative clause that restricts only providers leaves an unresolved question. Under ordinary criminal-law principles a successful prosecution of a visiting under-21 trans person for using their own lawfully prescribed hormones, or of a parent accompanying them, would almost certainly fail, and no test case had resolved the question at the time of writing. For an under-21 trans traveller the practical reading is that carrying and using prescribed hormone treatment on the island sits inside the law's literal definition of a banned practice, and that enforcement risk is harassment-shaped rather than conviction-shaped: questioning, detention or investigation by hostile officials, with the answer arriving only after the fact. The law's protected class is anyone under 21 and does not on its face reach patients 21 or older.

The law was pushed through non-public hearings and is written with deliberate vagueness, so doctors and affirming parents who facilitate hormone treatment or top surgery risk prosecution, a reach that extends to the accompanying parents of a travelling trans teenager. It mandates campaigns by the education and health departments on the risks of trans-affirming care. The health secretary proposed amendments that would have allowed puberty blockers and the continuation of existing hormone treatment; the text as enacted stands. The territory's LGBT federation announced plans to challenge the ban in court.

A civil-liberties organisation urged the governor to veto the bill, which it said criminalises doctors and parents and creates two distinct categories of children divided by whether identity aligns with sex assigned at birth. Its policy counsel stated that the bill allows parents to authorise treatment where a child's identity aligns with the sex assigned at birth and prohibits them the same right where it does not. Its executive director said the measure discriminates against transgender people and denies the existence of trans children and youth. The bill was authored by the senate president and a senator, passed both chambers in April, was returned for amendments suggested by the health secretary that the organisation warned did not remedy the rights violations, and was re-approved and returned to the governor on 28 June. Opposition was registered by several professional bodies - physicians and surgeons, psychology, social work, professional counselling and the bar association - and by the territory's LGBT federation.

The territory amended its hate crime statutes in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics. The first hate crime charges in the territory's history were brought in 2020, after two men were charged in the murder of two transgender women on 22 April 2020; one confessed to the killings. In January 2021 the governor declared a state of emergency over ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals on the island.

Anti-discrimination coverage is partial. The 2013 law that passed, a senate bill signed 29 May 2013, was amended in the lower chamber to apply only to employment discrimination, so public facilities, housing, transit and business transactions are not covered. An earlier bill passed the lower chamber 43-6 in November 2009 with wider coverage, but the senate held no hearings and took no action after the senate president said it would not be approved.

Marriage recognition for same-sex couples was won through federal court rather than local statute. The challenge was filed in March 2014 as a named federal case, with intervention from a legal-aid organisation and a local campaign group, and in June 2014 four couples joined as plaintiffs, among them a former member of the territorial guard and two couples already married abroad in 2007 and on the mainland in 2012.

Consensual private sexual activity between adults is not criminalised. The territory's supreme court upheld the territory's sodomy ban in 2002; after the governing state's top court 2003 ruling invalidated state and territorial sodomy statutes covering consensual private acts, the territory amended its penal code in 2004 to remove private, non-commercial sexual activity between consenting adults from the statute.

In April 2019 the governor announced a bill on religious freedom principles alongside a conversion-therapy ban carrying an exemption for clergy acting in a pastoral capacity. LGBT advocates, among them a council president, criticised the pairing as opening the door to refusals of service on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and on 13 June 2019 the governor asked lawmakers to withdraw both measures. A 2017 religious freedom bill that would have allowed public businesses to refuse service to LGBTQ people was vetoed in February 2018.

PYF.blindSummary:
The territory is an overseas collectivity of the governing state, and that state's law governs justice and civil status in the territory while territorial institutions in the capital regulate much of daily life.

Gender-diverse healthcare in the territory is limited by the small number of specialists available locally. Under the vice-president, the territorial government tabled a social-security bill that would have fully reimbursed hormonal treatment with progesterone and testosterone, matching the governing state's mainland; after heated debate in the territorial assembly the bill did not obtain sufficient support and lapsed. For a trans visitor staying any length of time, the gap between the law on paper and the care actually reachable in the archipelago is the most concrete material constraint.

The mahu role, a traditional island-culture recognition of gender diversity in which individuals embody both male and female qualities and hold recognised standing, predates colonisation, and mahu and rae-rae are visible across the islands in daily life. Reporting from a travel publication in July 2025 described this openness as ingrained in the culture rather than secured by law, noting that a visiting gay couple checked online whether the destination was safe before travelling and found mainstream inclusivity and acceptance operating without pride flags or organised protest. The 118-island territory has no Pride movement to speak of, which visitors read either as reassurance or as evidence that visibility is tolerated rather than defended.
PYF.blindTangential:
The territory's prisons fall under the governing state's national detention framework rather than territorial rules, so a trans visitor detained in the territory is housed under national provisions rather than any territorial arrangement.

Some trans residents, including rae-rae, face rejection from their families and leave for the governing state's mainland to obtain specialised services the territory cannot provide.

The territory hosted its first international LGBTQIA+ rights colloquium in 2023, bringing territorial government and church representatives together with the territory's university.

SHN.blindSummary:
The territory comprises a main island and two smaller constituent islands, all dependent island territories. The governing state's legislation reaches them only where extended by order, so the territory's own ordinances and institutions, not that state's law, determine what a visitor encounters. No transgender-specific criminal, documentation, screening, facilities, custody, care or violence provision is documented in territory law.

Consensual same-sex activity has been lawful since 2001, and the age of consent is equalised at 16 across the three constituent islands. No penalty provision specific to transgender people is documented.

The 2009 constitution order bans discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation and has been in force since 2009. It defines 'discriminatory' as affording different treatment to different persons on any ground such as sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, association with a national minority, property, age, disability, birth or other status. The enumerated grounds do not include gender reassignment, and no extension of the ban to gender reassignment is documented.

A 2015 equality ordinance defines 'gender reassignment' as an intended, current or past process, or part of such a process, for reassigning a person's sex by changing physiological or other attributes of sex, or the state of mind whereby a person psychologically identifies with a gender inconsistent with, or not culturally associated with, their assigned sex at birth. The same ordinance defines sexual orientation as a person's orientation towards persons of the same sex, the opposite sex, or either sex.

The territory's equality commission monitors human rights laws, promotes understanding of the importance of equality, and works towards the elimination of unlawful discrimination. It may conduct inquiries and investigations into persons suspected of having committed an unlawful act, including unlawful discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender reassignment.

Same-sex marriage is legal on one smaller constituent island under its 2016 marriage ordinance, approved by that island's council on 31 May 2016 by 5 votes to 0, signed and gazetted on 20 June 2016, and commenced on 1 January 2017. On the second smaller island it has been legal since 4 August 2017 under a 2017 ordinance, which defines marriage as the union of two persons regardless of sex and extends eligibility, formalities, rights and recognition to same-sex couples on equal terms with opposite-sex couples. On the main island it has been legal since 20 December 2017 under its own 2017 marriage ordinance; the first same-sex marriage there took place on 31 December 2018. No marriage provision specific to transgender people is documented.

Adoption by same-sex couples has been permitted since 2017. Under the main island's 2010 child-welfare ordinance, covering the main island and the second smaller island, and the other smaller island's 2011 child-welfare ordinance, single and married people may adopt regardless of sexual orientation. No adoption provision specific to transgender people is documented.

Protection against discrimination sits at two levels: the 2009 constitution order's enumerated grounds, which cover sex and sexual orientation but not gender reassignment, and the 2015 ordinance, which supplies a definition of gender reassignment and gives the equality commission jurisdiction over it. A visitor presenting a passport of the governing state with a changed gender marker can expect it to be treated as valid in the territory. No local statute or instrument giving effect to that recognition is identified in the available sources.

Visibility is low. A resident account published in 2009 described virtually no information about gay life in the territory and no visible social scene, with privacy as the everyday norm; the account attributed this partly to a population in which roughly two-thirds of residents are not originally from the islands, leaving full-citizen status holders a demographic minority. VGB.blindSummary:
Same-sex intimacy has not been a criminal offence in the territory since January 2001, when the governing state's highest court of appeal ordered the repeal of the sodomy laws across the territory and four other remaining island territories in the region after the local legislatures declined to act. The change came by order of that court rather than by enactment of the local legislature; a local legislator said at the time that 'there is nothing we can do'.

The territory stands under the governing state's constitutional framework, and measures of that state's parliament extend to it only when brought into force by an order of that state. A trans visitor should not assume that the governing state's discrimination and service-access protections, including its equality act and the 2025 single-sex-services code, are available in the territory by default; any such protection must be traced to local legislation or to a specific extension order.

Whether a marriage between two people of the same sex validly contracted elsewhere is recognised under local law remains contested rather than settled. The case testing whether the governing state's marriage of a married couple is valid locally was still running when, on 29 July 2022, a local church council lost its bid to appeal the case-management orders of a judge, as reported by a local news outlet. That refusal cleared a procedural obstacle and left the proceedings in place; it is not a ruling on recognition. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be classed locally as same-sex cannot rely on recognition being settled.
